 The missing link
 By  Asif Javed 
 02 November, 2026 
 Pakistan’s economic management has long revolved around familiar targets including reducing inflation, narrowing the fiscal deficit, stabilising the rupee and rebuilding foreign exchange reserves.
 STABILISATION & PROSPERITY 
 P akistan’s economic management has long revolved around familiar targets including reducing inflation, narrowing the fiscal deficit, stabilising the rupee and rebuilding foreign exchange reserves.
 These objectives are essential for an economy that has repeatedly faced balance-of-payments crises. Yet one question remains: why has repeated stabilisation failed to translate consistently into sustained improvements in productivity, investment and household incomes?
 The 2026 Nobel Prize in Economic Sciences offers a useful lens for examining this puzzle. Its emphasis on the microeconomic foundations of macroeconomic stabilisation highlights an important principle: aggregate economic outcomes cannot be fully understood without examining how households and businesses make decisions and how their combined actions shape the economy.
 For Pakistan, the implication is significant. Economic policy must be judged not only by whether it achieves short-term targets, but also by whether it creates incentives for productive investment, employment and lasting prosperity.
 Pakistan’s recent economic performance illustrates the distinction. According to the Pakistan Economic Survey 2025–26, GDP growth increased from 3.18 per cent in FY2024–25 to a provisional 3.70 per cent in FY2025–26. Industrial activity improved, with large-scale manufacturing growing by 6.11 per cent.
 Yet the recovery remains incomplete. Annual consumer inflation rose to 10.26 per cent in September 2026, after prices rose 1.27 per cent during the month. For households, the distinction between lower inflation and lower prices is crucial as even when inflation moderates, the accumulated increase in the cost of living does not disappear.
 These figures reveal two different dimensions of economic performance. Output can expand while households continue to face pressure on purchasing power. Industrial production can recover without necessarily generating sufficient productive employment or sustained improvements in real wages.
 The question, therefore, is not simply whether the economy is growing. It is how that growth is being generated, who benefits from it, and whether it creates the foundations for further expansion.
 Consider a business deciding whether to establish a factory or expand an existing one. Its decision depends not only on interest rates and current demand, but also on electricity costs, taxation, access to imported machinery, exchange-rate risks and the predictability of government policy.
 When these conditions are uncertain, postponing investment can be a rational response. Businesses may prefer short-term activities or hold liquid assets rather than commit resources to expanding productive capacity.
 When many firms make similar decisions, the consequences become macroeconomic as investment weakens, productivity growth slows, employment opportunities diminish and the economy becomes 
 less competitive.
 Pakistan’s fiscal position illustrates why incentives matter. The IMF reported that the country’s tax revenue ratio, including provincial taxes and the petroleum levy, reached 12.3 per cent of GDP in FY2024–25. This represented progress, but remained low compared with peer countries.
 Broadening the tax base is essential. However, repeatedly imposing additional burdens on businesses already within the formal tax system, without adequately expanding compliance elsewhere, risks discouraging investment and reinforcing incentives for informality.
 Broadening the tax base is essential. However, repeatedly imposing additional burdens on businesses already within the formal tax system, without adequately expanding compliance elsewhere, risks discouraging investment and reinforcing incentives for informality A more sustainable approach would combine stronger enforcement with simpler rules, fewer unjustified exemptions and predictable taxation. The objective should be to make formal, productive economic activity more attractive rather than merely extracting additional revenue from the existing tax base.
 Monetary and fiscal policies remain central to economic stability, but their design matters. Higher interest rates can restrain excessive demand and anchor inflationary expectations. Yet when inflation is driven partly by imported energy, supply disruptions or administered price adjustments, monetary tightening cannot directly resolve the underlying supply constraints.
 Similarly, fiscal adjustment can improve public finances, but its economic consequences depend on how it is achieved. Broadening the tax base and reducing inefficient expenditure can strengthen the state’s capacity to invest. Indiscriminate cuts to development spending, by contrast, may weaken infrastructure, education and future productive capacity.
 The objective is not to abandon fiscal discipline or monetary restraint. The goal is to ensure that pursuing stability supports investment and productivity rather than unnecessarily constraining them.
 Economic policy also shapes household decisions. When food, electricity and transport become more expensive, families have less income available for other consumption and investment in education or healthcare. Uncertainty may force households to postpone important expenditure or reduce their savings. Individually, these 
 responses are understandable. Collectively, they 
 can weaken domestic 
 demand, reduce business revenues and slow economic activity.
 This is particularly important in Pakistan, where increases in essential living costs can absorb a substantial share of household budgets. Policies that improve aggregate indicators but leave households with persistently weak purchasing power may also undermine the demand needed to sustain business expansion.
 Well-targeted social protection can help vulnerable families withstand economic adjustment without sacrificing the nutrition, education and healthcare essential to their future productivity. Human capital is not separate from economic management; it is a foundation of sustainable growth.
 Pakistan does not need to choose between stabilisation and growth. It needs to connect them. Monetary policy must support price stability; fiscal policy must place public finances on a sustainable footing; energy reform must improve reliability and competitiveness; and trade policy must encourage exports and higher-value production. These policies should operate within a predictable framework that enables households and businesses to make decisions over longer horizons.
 Every major reform should therefore be assessed against two questions: does it restore stability today and does it improve the economy’s capacity to produce, invest and create employment tomorrow?
 The broader lesson from the microeconomic foundations of macroeconomic stabilisation is that economic outcomes emerge from people and institutions responding to incentives, constraints and expectations. Aggregate targets matter, but their achievement is not an end in itself.
 Pakistan’s challenge is to build an economic system in which stability encourages investment,investment raises productivity, and productivity generates better jobs and higher real incomes.
 The ultimate test of stabilisation is not simply whether the numbers improve. It is whether the resulting economic environment enables households and businesses to make decisions that collectively deliver lasting prosperity.
 The writer is an associate research fellow at the Sustainable Development Policy Institute (SDPI), Islamabad.
